title: 🏛️ 8 Macro-Ages & 28 Literary Periods
subtitle: Chronological staircase dates, student overviews, memory tricks & exam cues

items.title: Era Step 1: Ancient & Classical World (c. 800 BCE – 525 CE)

fields.label: Era Title
fields.value: Ancient & Classical World

fields.label: Date Span
fields.value: c. 800 BCE – 525 CE

fields.label: Simple Story / Student Overview
fields.value: Before English even existed, the foundations of storytelling, theatre, and literary criticism were laid in Ancient Greece, Rome, and India. Greek poets like Homer sang grand heroic epics (The Iliad and The Odyssey), Athenian playwrights like Sophocles invented tragedy on stage, and philosophers like Plato and Aristotle asked the big questions: 'Why do we love stories?' and 'What makes a great tragedy?' Later, Roman writers like Virgil, Ovid, and Horace adapted these Greek models into Latin—and centuries later, English writers copied them!

fields.label: Memory Trick / Exam Hook
fields.value: Think of Step 1 as the 'Root System' of a tree: every time Shakespeare, Milton, or T.S. Eliot writes a play or epic, they are borrowing stories and rules from Greece and Rome.

items.title: Era Step 2: The Medieval Age (c. 500 – 1500)

fields.label: Era Title
fields.value: The Medieval Age

fields.label: Simple Story / Student Overview
fields.value: After the Roman Empire fell, Germanic tribes (Angles and Saxons) settled in Britain, bringing Old English and warrior poems like Beowulf. Then in 1066, French-speaking Normans conquered England, blending French courtly romance (King Arthur and his knights) with English speech. By the late 1300s, Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in vivid London Middle English—proving that everyday English could tell funny, realistic, and unforgettable stories about ordinary people.

fields.label: Memory Trick / Exam Hook
fields.value: 3 Big Turning Points: 450 (Anglo-Saxons arrive) → 1066 (Norman Conquest brings French) → 1476 (Caxton's Printing Press).

items.title: Era Step 3: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era (c. 1500 – 1660)

fields.label: Era Title
fields.value: The Renaissance & Early Modern Era

fields.label: Simple Story / Student Overview
fields.value: 'Renaissance' simply means 'Rebirth'. People rediscovered ancient Greek and Roman books, questioned old authorities, printed English Bibles, and celebrated human potential. Under Queen Elizabeth I (1558–1603) and King James I (1603–1625), London exploded with public playhouses where Christopher Marlowe, William Shakespeare, Ben Jonson, and John Webster staged thrilling tragedies and comedies. Meanwhile, John Donne invented clever 'Metaphysical' love and religious poetry, and John Milton lived through the English Civil War to write greatest English epic, Paradise Lost.

fields.label: Memory Trick / Exam Hook
fields.value: Tudor (Humanists) → Elizabethan (Sonnets & Marlowe/Shakespeare) → Jacobean (Dark Tragedy, Donne, 1611 Bible) → Caroline/Puritan (Theatres closed 1642, Milton).

items.title: Era Step 4: The Long Eighteenth Century (1660 – 1798)

fields.label: Era Title
fields.value: The Long Eighteenth Century

fields.label: Simple Story / Student Overview
fields.value: In 1660, King Charles II returned from France ('The Restoration') and immediately reopened London's theatres—bringing witty 'Comedies of Manners' and the first professional women playwrights and novelists like Aphra Behn. Writers grew tired of religious wars and valued Reason, Order, Wit, and Polite Society ('Neoclassicism'). In the early 1700s, Alexander Pope and Jonathan Swift wrote brilliant satires, Addison and Steele started daily newspapers in London coffee-houses, Daniel Defoe, Samuel Richardson, and Henry Fielding invented the English Novel, and Dr. Samuel Johnson wrote the first great English Dictionary (1755).

fields.label: Memory Trick / Exam Hook
fields.value: 1660 (King & Theatres return) → 1700–1745 (Pope & Swift's Satire + Coffee-Houses) → 1745–1798 (Dr. Johnson + Rise of Gothic & Emotion).

items.title: Era Step 5: The Nineteenth Century (1798 – 1901)

fields.label: Era Title
fields.value: The Nineteenth Century

fields.label: Simple Story / Student Overview
fields.value: In 1798, William Wordsworth and S.T. Coleridge published Lyrical Ballads, launching the Romantic Movement: instead of city coffee-houses and strict rules, poets celebrated wild Nature, childhood, imagination, and revolution (Blake, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley, Keats, alongside Jane Austen and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein). Then, under Queen Victoria (1837–1901), trains, factories, Empire, and Charles Darwin's theory of evolution transformed society. Novelists like Charles Dickens, the Brontë sisters, George Eliot, and Thomas Hardy wrote deeply moving novels about poverty, morality, women's lives, and religious doubt—while in America (Emerson, Whitman, Melville, Dickinson) and India (Derozio, Toru Dutt, Bankimchandra) vibrant new literatures blossomed.

fields.label: Memory Trick / Exam Hook
fields.value: 1798–1837 is Heart, Nature & Imagination (Romantics); 1837–1901 is Trains, Factories, Faith vs. Science & the Great Novel (Victorians).

items.title: Era Step 6: The Modernist & Inter-War Era (1901 – 1945)

fields.label: Era Title
fields.value: The Modernist & Inter-War Era

fields.label: Simple Story / Student Overview
fields.value: The 20th century opened with Sigmund Freud's psychology, Einstein's physics, and the devastating shock of World War I (1914–1918). Writers felt the old Victorian ways of telling a neat, linear story no longer matched a broken modern world. 'Make It New!' became the cry of Modernism. In a single miracle year—1922—James Joyce published Ulysses and T.S. Eliot published The Waste Land, while Virginia Woolf pioneered 'stream-of-consciousness' fiction. Meanwhile, in India during the 1930s Gandhian movement, Mulk Raj Anand, R.K. Narayan, and Raja Rao gave birth to the classic Indian English novel.

fields.label: Memory Trick / Exam Hook
fields.value: Remember the Miracle Year 1922 (Ulysses + The Waste Land + Jacob's Room) and the Indian Trio of 1935–1938 (Anand, Narayan, Raja Rao).

items.title: Era Step 7: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary Era (1945 – Present)

fields.label: Era Title
fields.value: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary Era

fields.label: Date Span
fields.value: 1945 – Present

fields.label: Simple Story / Student Overview
fields.value: After World War II, the Holocaust, and the end of the British Empire (Indian Independence in 1947), literature became truly global and experimental. On stage, Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot (1953) showed the 'Theatre of the Absurd', while John Osborne's Look Back in Anger (1956) launched 'Angry Young Men' drama. Novelists mixed history with fantasy ('Magic Realism' and 'Historiographic Metafiction'), and writers from India (Nissim Ezekiel, Kamala Das, Anita Desai, Salman Rushdie, Amitav Ghosh, Arundhati Roy), Africa (Chinua Achebe, Wole Soyinka, Ngugi), the Caribbean (Derek Walcott, V.S. Naipaul), Canada (Margaret Atwood), and Australia (Patrick White) won the world's biggest literary prizes.

fields.label: Memory Trick / Exam Hook
fields.value: After 1945, the 'Empire Writes Back': British postmodernism meets Indian, African, Caribbean, and American multicultural masterpieces.

items.title: Era Step 8: Criticism, Theory, Language & India Story (Thematic & Methodological)

fields.label: Era Title
fields.value: Criticism, Theory, Language & India Story

fields.label: Date Span
fields.value: Thematic & Methodological

fields.label: Simple Story / Student Overview
fields.value: Roughly 35% to 40% of the UGC NET English paper tests your toolkit as a teacher and scholar (Units V to X). Instead of just asking 'who wrote which novel', these units ask: How do we read and interpret texts (New Criticism, Structuralism, Deconstruction, Feminism, Marxism, Postcolonialism, Ecocriticism)? How did English come to India through laws like the 1813 Charter Act, Macaulay's 1835 Minute, and Wood's 1854 Despatch? How do we teach English in classrooms (ELT methods & linguistics)? And how do we write academic research papers (MLA style, thesis writing, qualitative vs. quantitative research)?

fields.label: Memory Trick / Exam Hook
fields.value: Think of Step 8 as your 'Scholar's Lens': the critical theories, Indian education policies, language pedagogy, and research tools that earn easy, direct marks.

items.title: PER-1.01: Archaic Greece (c. 800–480 BCE)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Archaic Greece

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: The dawn of Western poetry (c. 800–500 BCE). Homer composed The Iliad (about the Trojan War and Achilles' wrath) and The Odyssey (Odysseus's 10-year journey home), Hesiod wrote Theogony and Works and Days, and Sappho sang personal lyric poems on the island of Lesbos.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Oral-formulaic heroic epic (Iliad, Odyssey); didactic/cosmogonic poetry (Theogony, Works and Days); Sapphic monodic lyric vs. Pindaric choral ode (strophe, antistrophe, epode).

items.title: PER-1.02: Classical Greece (Attic Age) (c. 480–323 BCE)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Classical Greece (Attic Age)

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: The Golden Age of Athens (500–323 BCE). Democracy, theatre festivals, and philosophy flourished. Aeschylus (Oresteia), Sophocles (Oedipus Rex, Antigone), and Euripides (Medea) wrote the greatest Greek tragedies; Aristophanes (The Frogs) wrote sharp comic plays; and Plato & Aristotle laid the foundation of literary criticism.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Attic Tragedy (Oresteia, Oedipus Rex, Medea, Bacchae); Old Comedy (Frogs, Clouds, Lysistrata); Classical Historiography; Plato's Republic/Ion vs. Aristotle's Poetics.

items.title: PER-1.03: Hellenistic / Alexandrian Greece (323–31 BCE)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Hellenistic / Alexandrian Greece

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: After Alexander the Great's conquests (323–31 BCE), Greek culture spread across the Mediterranean with its great library at Alexandria. Callimachus championed short, polished verse, Theocritus invented pastoral poetry (shepherds singing in nature), and Apollonius wrote the epic Argonautica.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Pastoral idyll (Theocritus's Idylls); Alexandrian learned aesthetic (Callimachus); New Comedy (Menander); Longinus's On the Sublime (hypsos, 5 sources of sublimity).

items.title: PER-1.04: Roman Republic (c. 250–27 BCE)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Roman Republic

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Rome began adapting Greek drama and philosophy into Latin (c. 240–27 BCE). Plautus and Terence wrote lively domestic comedies that later inspired Shakespeare and Ben Jonson; Lucretius wrote the philosophical poem On the Nature of Things; Catullus wrote passionate lyrics; and Cicero mastered political and rhetorical prose.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Roman New Comedy (miles gloriosus, double plots influencing Shakespeare & Jonson); Epicurean philosophical epic (De Rerum Natura); Neoteric lyric (Catullus); Ciceronian rhetoric.

items.title: PER-1.05: Roman Augustan (Golden Age) (27 BCE – 14 CE)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Roman Augustan (Golden Age)

fields.label: Date Span
fields.value: 27 BCE – 14 CE

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Under Emperor Augustus (27 BCE – 14 CE), Rome produced its greatest poetry. Virgil wrote the national epic The Aeneid and pastoral Eclogues; Horace wrote his Odes, Satires, and the critical guide Ars Poetica ('ut pictura poesis', 'in medias res'); and Ovid wrote Metamorphoses—Shakespeare's favourite book of myths.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Virgil's Eclogues, Georgics, Aeneid; Ovid's Metamorphoses & Heroides (primary myth source for Renaissance); Horatian satire, odes & Ars Poetica (decorum, in medias res, dulce et utile).

items.title: PER-1.06: Roman Imperial (Silver Age) (14 – c. 180 CE)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Roman Imperial (Silver Age)

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: During the later Roman Empire (14–300 CE), Seneca wrote bloody philosophical revenge tragedies (which directly inspired Elizabethan revenge plays like The Spanish Tragedy and Hamlet), Juvenal wrote fierce 'Juvenalian' satire, Longinus wrote On the Sublime, and Apuleius wrote The Golden Ass.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Senecan closet revenge tragedy (Thyestes, Phaedra, Medea); Juvenalian indignatio satire (Satire X); Martial's epigrams; Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria; Plutarch's Parallel Lives (via North 1579).

items.title: PER-1.07: Late Antiquity & Patristic Transition (c. 180 – 525 CE)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Late Antiquity & Patristic Transition

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: As the Roman world turned Christian (c. 300–525 CE), St. Augustine wrote the first great spiritual autobiography (Confessions) and City of God, St. Jerome translated the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate), and Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison—later translated by King Alfred, Chaucer, and Queen Elizabeth I.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Latin Vulgate Bible (Jerome); spiritual autobiography (Augustine's Confessions, City of God); Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (translated by Alfred, Chaucer, Elizabeth I).

items.title: PER-2.08: Old English / Anglo-Saxon Period (c. 650–1066)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Old English / Anglo-Saxon Period

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: From 450 to 1066 CE, Anglo-Saxon poets composed heroic and Christian verse in Old English using alliteration and 'kennings' (poetic compounds like 'whale-road' for the sea). Remember the epic Beowulf, elegies like The Wanderer and The Seafarer, the religious poets Caedmon and Cynewulf, and King Alfred's prose translations.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: 4 poetic codices (Nowell/Beowulf, Junius, Exeter, Vercelli); alliterative verse, caesura & kennings; elegies (Wanderer, Seafarer, Deor); Bede's Historia (731); Alfredian prose translations.

items.title: PER-2.09: Early Middle English & Anglo-Norman (1066–1340)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Early Middle English & Anglo-Norman

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Matter of Britain / Arthurian foundation (Historia Regum Britanniae -> Roman de Brut -> Layamon's Brut); Ormulum; Ancrene Wisse; Owl and the Nightingale; Havelok the Dane; King Horn.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Matter of Britain / Arthurian foundation (Historia Regum Britanniae -> Roman de Brut -> Layamon's Brut); Ormulum; Ancrene Wisse; Owl and the Nightingale; Havelok the Dane; King Horn.

items.title: PER-2.10: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) (1340–1400)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century)

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Estates satire & frame narrative (Canterbury Tales); rhyme royal & heroic couplet; Alliterative Revival (Piers Plowman A/B/C, Sir Gawain, Pearl); Wycliffe's Bible; earliest female-authored English prose.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Estates satire & frame narrative (Canterbury Tales); rhyme royal & heroic couplet; Alliterative Revival (Piers Plowman A/B/C, Sir Gawain, Pearl); Wycliffe's Bible; earliest female-authored English prose.

items.title: PER-2.11: 15th-Century Transition, Drama & Early Print (1400–1500)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: 15th-Century Transition, Drama & Early Print

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: English & Scottish Chaucerians (Kingis Quair, Testament of Cresseid); Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (1485, printed by Caxton); Mystery Cycles (York, Wakefield/Secunda Pastorum, Chester, N-Town) & Everyman.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: English & Scottish Chaucerians (Kingis Quair, Testament of Cresseid); Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (1485, printed by Caxton); Mystery Cycles (York, Wakefield/Secunda Pastorum, Chester, N-Town) & Everyman.

items.title: PER-3.12: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation (c. 1500–1558)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Christian Humanism (More's Utopia 1516 Latin / 1551 English); Tyndale Bible (1526); Tottel's Miscellany (1557) introducing Petrarchan sonnet (Wyatt) and English sonnet + blank verse (Surrey).

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Christian Humanism (More's Utopia 1516 Latin / 1551 English); Tyndale Bible (1526); Tottel's Miscellany (1557) introducing Petrarchan sonnet (Wyatt) and English sonnet + blank verse (Surrey).

items.title: PER-3.13: Elizabethan Period (1558–1603)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Elizabethan Period

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Queen Elizabeth I's reign (1558–1603) was the golden age of English drama and poetry. Edmund Spenser wrote The Faerie Queene, Sir Philip Sidney wrote Astrophel and Stella and An Apology for Poetry, the 'University Wits' (Lyly, Peele, Greene, Lodge, Nashe, Kyd, and Christopher Marlowe) transformed the stage, and William Shakespeare began his career.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Pastoral & national epic (Shepheardes Calender 1579, Faerie Queene 1590/96); 1590s sonnet craze (Astrophel and Stella, Amoretti); University Wits; Revenge Tragedy; Shakespeare's comedies/histories; Sidney's Apology (1595).

items.title: PER-3.14: Jacobean Period (1603–1625)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Jacobean Period

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Under King James I (1603–1625), literature became more probing, psychological, and dark. Shakespeare wrote his great tragedies (Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth) and late romances (The Tempest); Ben Jonson perfected the 'Comedy of Humours' (Volpone, The Alchemist); John Webster wrote chilling revenge tragedies (The Duchess of Malfi); John Donne led the Metaphysical poets; Francis Bacon wrote his Essays; and the 1611 King James Bible appeared.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: High Shakespearean tragedy & First Folio (1623); Jonson's 1616 Works & Comedy of Humours; Jacobean Revenge Tragedy (Duchess of Malfi, White Devil); Metaphysical conceits (Donne); King James Bible (1611).

items.title: PER-3.15: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum (1625–1660)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Caroline & Commonwealth / Puritan Interregnum

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Sacred Metaphysicals (The Temple 1633, Silex Scintillans 1650); Cavalier carpe diem lyric (Hesperides 1648); 1642 closure of theatres; Milton's Areopagitica (1644); Hobbes's Leviathan (1651); Anne Bradstreet (1650).

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Sacred Metaphysicals (The Temple 1633, Silex Scintillans 1650); Cavalier carpe diem lyric (Hesperides 1648); 1642 closure of theatres; Milton's Areopagitica (1644); Hobbes's Leviathan (1651); Anne Bradstreet (1650).

items.title: PER-4.16: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden) (1660–1700)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Restoration Age (Age of Dryden)

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: 1660 reopening of theatres & actresses on stage; Heroic Tragedy vs. Comedy of Manners (Country Wife, Way of the World) & Collier controversy (1698); Paradise Lost (1667/1674); Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress (1678); Oroonoko (1688).

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: 1660 reopening of theatres & actresses on stage; Heroic Tragedy vs. Comedy of Manners (Country Wife, Way of the World) & Collier controversy (1698); Paradise Lost (1667/1674); Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress (1678); Oroonoko (1688).

items.title: PER-4.17: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) (1700–1745)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift)

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Scriblerus & Kit-Cat Clubs; Mock-epic & Tory satire (Rape of the Lock 1712/14, Dunciad 1728/43, Gulliver's Travels 1726, Modest Proposal 1729); Tatler (1709) & Spectator (1711); Rise of Novel (Defoe, Pamela 1740 vs. Shamela/Joseph Andrews).

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Scriblerus & Kit-Cat Clubs; Mock-epic & Tory satire (Rape of the Lock 1712/14, Dunciad 1728/43, Gulliver's Travels 1726, Modest Proposal 1729); Tatler (1709) & Spectator (1711); Rise of Novel (Defoe, Pamela 1740 vs. Shamela/Joseph Andrews).

items.title: PER-4.18: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition (1745–1798)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: From 1745 to 1798, strict Neoclassical rules gave way to deep human feeling ('Sensibility'), Gothic mystery, and interest in folk ballads. Dr. Samuel Johnson compiled his landmark Dictionary (1755), Rasselas (1759), and Lives of the Poets (1779–81), recorded by his biographer James Boswell. Laurence Sterne wrote the playful Tristram Shandy, Oliver Goldsmith and R.B. Sheridan revived stage comedy, Horace Walpole (The Castle of Otranto, 1764) and Ann Radcliffe invented the Gothic novel, and Thomas Gray, William Cowper, Robert Burns, and William Blake paved the way for Romanticism.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Johnson's Dictionary (1755), Shakespeare Preface (1765), Lives of the Poets (1779–81); Tristram Shandy (1759–67); Gothic novel (Castle of Otranto 1764, Mysteries of Udolpho 1794); Graveyard & Pre-Romantic lyric; Anti-sentimental comedy (1773/1777).

items.title: PER-5.19: British Romantic Period (1798–1837)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: British Romantic Period

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Triggered by the French Revolution and the 1798 publication of Lyrical Ballads by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Romanticism (1798–1837) celebrated nature, ordinary language, childhood, and the sublime imagination. Alongside the 'Lake Poets' (Wordsworth, Coleridge, Southey) came the younger rebels Lord Byron, Percy Bysshe Shelley, and John Keats; the brilliant novelists Jane Austen (Pride and Prejudice), Walter Scott (historical novels), and Mary Shelley (Frankenstein, 1818); and essayists Charles Lamb, William Hazlitt, and Thomas De Quincey.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Lyrical Ballads (1798/1800) & Biographia Literaria (1817); First vs. Second Generation Romantics; Keats's 1819 Odes & Negative Capability; Austen's 6 novels; Scott's Waverley historical novels; Frankenstein (1818/1831).

items.title: PER-5.20: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain (1837–1870)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Condition-of-England / Industrial Novels (Hard Times, North and South, Sybil); 1847 Bronte landmark year; Dramatic Monologue (Browning, Tennyson); Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (1848, The Germ); Sensation Fiction (Woman in White 1859–60).

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Condition-of-England / Industrial Novels (Hard Times, North and South, Sybil); 1847 Bronte landmark year; Dramatic Monologue (Browning, Tennyson); Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (1848, The Germ); Sensation Fiction (Woman in White 1859–60).

items.title: PER-5.21: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle (1870–1901)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: In the final decades of Victoria's reign (1870–1901), Victorian optimism darkened into scepticism, pessimism, and the 'Art for Art's Sake' (Aesthetic) movement. Thomas Hardy wrote tragic novels of Wessex (Tess of the d'Urbervilles, Jude the Obscure); Gerard Manley Hopkins invented 'sprung rhythm' (published posthumously in 1918); Walter Pater inspired Aestheticism; Oscar Wilde sparkled with The Picture of Dorian Gray (1890) and The Importance of Being Earnest (1895); and Robert Louis Stevenson, Bram Stoker (Dracula), and Arthur Conan Doyle created enduring gothic and detective classics.

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: Wessex tragic naturalism (Tess 1891, Jude 1895); Hopkins's sprung rhythm, inscape/instress (published 1918); Aestheticism ('Art for Art's Sake' — Pater's Renaissance 1873, Wilde's Dorian Gray 1890/91 & Earnest 1895); Imperial Gothic (Dracula 1897).

items.title: PER-5.22: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English (1794–1900)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: American Transcendentalism (Nature 1836, Walden 1854) & Dark Romanticism (Scarlet Letter 1850, Moby-Dick 1851); Leaves of Grass (1855); Slave Narratives; Early Indian English (Dean Mahomed 1794, Derozio 1827, Rajmohan's Wife 1864, Toru Dutt 1882).

fields.label: Official UGC NET Exam Cues
fields.value: American Transcendentalism (Nature 1836, Walden 1854) & Dark Romanticism (Scarlet Letter 1850, Moby-Dick 1851); Leaves of Grass (1855); Slave Narratives; Early Indian English (Dean Mahomed 1794, Derozio 1827, Rajmohan's Wife 1864, Toru Dutt 1882).

items.title: PER-6.23: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival (1901–1914)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview

items.title: PER-6.24: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation (1914–1945)

fields.value: WWI War Poets ('pity of war'); Annus Mirabilis 1922 (Ulysses, The Waste Land, Jacob's Room); Stream-of-consciousness (Mrs Dalloway 1925, To the Lighthouse 1927); Lawrence (Sons and Lovers 1913, Rainbow 1915, Women in Love 1920); 1930s MacSpaunday poets.

items.title: PER-6.25: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era (1901–1947)

fields.label: Period Title
fields.value: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era

fields.value: Imagism & Lost Generation (Great Gatsby 1925, Sun Also Rises 1926, Sound and the Fury 1929); Harlem Renaissance (Their Eyes Were Watching God 1937); Tagore's Gitanjali (1912/1913 Nobel); 1930s Indian English Novel Trio (Untouchable 1935, Swami and Friends 1935, Kanthapura 1938).

fields.label: Date Span

fields.label: Simple Story / Overview
fields.value: Units V to X cover the theoretical, historical, linguistic, and methodological pillars of English Studies: Unit V (Linguistics, Phonetics, Pragmatics, Second Language Acquisition & ELT Methodology), Unit VI (Institutional History of English in India from 1780 to NEP 2020), Unit VII (Cultural Studies: Birmingham CCCS, Richard Hoggart, Raymond Williams, Stuart Hall, Popular Culture), Unit VIII (Literary Criticism from Plato, Aristotle, Horace, and Longinus to Dryden, Johnson, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Arnold, Eliot, I.A. Richards, and F.R. Leavis), Unit IX (Post-WWII Literary Theory: Russian Formalism, Structuralism, Poststructuralism/Deconstruction, Psychoanalysis, Marxism, Feminism/Gender/Queer Theory, Postcolonialism, New Historicism, Ecocriticism), and Unit X (Research Methods in English).
